Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ and metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. An external scalar datum consists of a spin-zero species assigned a mass $m>0$ and elastic two-particle threshold $s=4m^2$. This is a mathematical input package; it does not construct a one-particle scattering state or a scattering matrix. For real on-shell momenta $p_1,p_2$ incoming and $p_3,p_4$ outgoing, with $p_j^2=-m^2$ and $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$, define

$$s=-(p_1+p_2)^2,\qquad t=-(p_1-p_3)^2,\qquad u=-(p_1-p_4)^2.$$

Then $s+t+u=4m^2$. The forward slice is the complex-valued function $A(s)=\mathcal A(s,0,4m^2-s)$ obtained by analytically continuing the identical-scalar $2\to2$ amplitude to $t=0$. The crossing action on this slice is $s\mapsto4m^2-s$, which exchanges $s$ and $u$. Assume $A(s)=A(4m^2-s)$ wherever both sides are defined.

For context, define the physical elastic kinematic region

$$\mathscr P_m=\{(s,t,u)\in\mathbb R^3:s>4m^2,\;-(s-4m^2)\le t\le0,\;u=4m^2-s-t\}.$$

When supplied, the full physical amplitude is a map $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{phys}}:\mathscr P_m\to\mathbb C$; its analytic continuation used in the forward data above is a separate supplied part of the input, with upper boundary value $A(s+i0)=\mathcal A_{\mathrm{phys}}(s,0,4m^2-s)$ for $s>4m^2$. For $(s,t,u)\in\mathscr P_m$, put $x=1+2t/(s-4m^2)\in[-1,1]$. For each integer $\ell\ge0$, define the normalized Legendre polynomial $P_\ell:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ by

$$P_\ell(x)=\frac{1}{2^\ell\ell!}\frac{d^\ell}{dx^\ell}(x^2-1)^\ell,$$

and let $a_\ell:(4m^2,\infty)\to\mathbb C$ be the complex partial-wave coefficient function in this channel. When a full partial-wave expansion is asserted on the physical angular interval, require the partial sums of the right-hand side below to converge uniformly in $x\in[-1,1]$ for each fixed $s>4m^2$ to the supplied physical amplitude. Use the normalization

$$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{phys}}(s,t,u)=16\pi\sqrt{\frac{s}{s-4m^2}}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)P_\ell\!\left(1+\frac{2t}{s-4m^2}\right)a_\ell(s),\qquad P_\ell(1)=1.$$

For the forward sign alone, convergence of the series at $x=1$ suffices. The downstream forward-positivity result uses the optical-theorem sign $\operatorname{Im}A(s+i0)\ge0$ for $s>4m^2$ as input; a full partial-wave realization is not inferred from this definition. In the displayed normalization, the sign follows if the forward series converges and the supplied partial waves obey $\operatorname{Im}a_\ell(s)\ge|a_\ell(s)|^2\ge0$ for every $s>4m^2$ and every $\ell$.

Put $\nu_0=2m^2$ and $v=s-2m^2$, so $u-2m^2=-v$. Choose finitely many real numbers $p_j\in(0,4m^2)\setminus\{2m^2\}$ and real residues $r_j$, and set

$$P(s)=\sum_j\left(\frac{r_j}{s-p_j}+\frac{r_j}{4m^2-p_j-s}\right).$$

Each summand pair is the real simple-pole principal part at $s=p_j$ and its $s\leftrightarrow u$ crossing partner; hence $P(4m^2-s)=P(s)$. These poles lie off the two-particle cuts. Define the pole-subtracted forward function $B(v)=A(2m^2+v)-P(2m^2+v)$. Assume $B$ is holomorphic on

$$\Omega_{\nu_0}=\mathbb C\setminus\bigl((-\infty,-\nu_0]\cup[\nu_0,\infty)\bigr),$$

real analytic there, meaning $B(\overline v)=\overline{B(v)}$, and has finite upper and lower boundary values on both cuts except at their endpoints. Here the two-particle gap is the open interval $(-\nu_0,\nu_0)$ in the $v$ variable; no massless pole or cut reaches the forward point $t=0$.

Require additionally that $B$ extends continuously from each open half-plane onto every compact segment of either real cut bank avoiding $\pm\nu_0$. This is an extra admissibility assumption on the supplied data, not a consequence of finite pointwise boundary values or a claim about every quantum field theory. 

Assume the exact high-energy condition $B(w)=o(|w|^2)$ uniformly as $|w|\to\infty$ in the closed upper half-plane, including upper cut-bank limits. In particular this holds on the large upper semicircles after any fixed bounded horizontal translation. For $\nu\ge\nu_0$, define the absorptive density $\rho(\nu)=\operatorname{Im}B(\nu+i0)$. Require $\rho$ to be nonnegative and Riemann integrable on every compact subinterval of $[\nu_0,\infty)$, and require $\int_{\nu_0}^{\infty}\rho(\nu)\nu^{-3}\,d\nu$ to converge as a finite improper Riemann integral. For every real $v$ with $|v|<\nu_0$, require the integrals along both sides of the two cuts of $[B(x)-B(0)]/[x^2(x-v)]$, with boundary values taken from the upper and lower half-planes, to exist as finite improper Riemann limits. Require also that the small endpoint arcs at $\pm\nu_0$ for this integrand vanish in the contour limit. Since $P$ is real off its poles, $\rho(\nu)=\operatorname{Im}A(2m^2+\nu+i0)$ for $\nu>\nu_0$ on the right cut.

The normalized forward Taylor coefficients are $c_n=B^{(2n)}(0)/(2n)!$ for integers $n\ge1$. They have units $(\text{mass})^{-4n}$; $\nu_0$ has units $(\text{mass})^2$. No sign is assigned here to a generic off-shell Lagrangian coefficient.

derivations.claim: Set $s=2m^2+v$. Then the crossed value is $u=4m^2-s=2m^2-v$. By [A1], $A(2m^2+v)=A(2m^2-v)$ and $P(2m^2+v)=P(2m^2-v)$. Subtracting the pole terms gives $B(v)=B(-v)$.
Differentiate $B(-v)=B(v)$ at $v=0$. The chain rule gives $-B'(0)=B'(0)$; since $2\ne0$ in $\mathbb C$, $B'(0)=0$.

step 2.1: the derivative at the subtraction point is exactly zero.

The statement assumes m>0 and does not take a zero-gap limit.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: the identity is asserted wherever both crossed values are defined, including the subtraction point under its neighborhood hypothesis.
step 1.1: one arbitrary admissible v is handled by direct substitution, with no choice from a family.

The lemma is a one-way implication.

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc

$$D(a,R)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta-a|<R\}.$$

If $0<r<R$, $|z-a|<r$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, then

$$f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and fix $z\in U$. Define

$$g(\zeta)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{f(\zeta)-f(z)}{\zeta-z},&\zeta\ne z,\\[6pt]f'(z),&\zeta=z.\end{cases}$$

Then $g$ is continuous on $U$ and holomorphic on $U\setminus\{z\}$. No holomorphy at the filled point $z$ is asserted.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open and star-shaped, let $p\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and holomorphic on $U\setminus\{p\}$. Then $f$ has a primitive on $U$, and for every closed rectifiable contour $\gamma$ in $U$,

$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0.$$

A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Let $f$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval $[a,R]$ with $R>a$. The improper integral over the right-unbounded interval is
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,dx,$$
provided this limit exists as a finite real number. In that case the improper integral **converges**; otherwise it diverges. In particular, a limit of $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ is divergence, not convergence to an extended-real value.

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[R,b]$ with $R<b$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{R\to-\infty}\int_R^b f(x)\,dx$$
under the same finite-limit convention. All finite integrals use the oriented convention.

If the improper integrals of $f$ and $g$ converge over the same one-ended interval and $r,s\in\mathbb R$, then
$$\int(rf+sg)=r\int f+s\int g.$$
The same formula holds for mixed improper integrals when every singular-end piece of both integrals converges separately.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
FALSE: a nonnegative Riemann integrable function on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically zero on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is A continuous $f \ge 0$ on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically $0$
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$, $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Suppose $0\le f\le g$ eventually toward a singular end. If the improper integral of $g$ converges there, then the integral of $f$ converges. If instead $|f|\le g$ eventually and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges absolutely and hence converges.

The same assertions hold separately at $+\infty$, at $-\infty$, and at either finite singular endpoint.

derivations.claim: Apply [F3] to $B$ on any circle centered at $0$ with radius $r<\nu_0$. Expanding $(\zeta-v)^{-1}=\sum_{j\ge0}v^j\zeta^{-j-1}$ uniformly on that circle for $|v|<r$ gives the Taylor series of $B$ near $0$. By [F2], every odd coefficient vanishes. Hence $H(v):=(B(v)-B(0))/v^2$ has a holomorphic extension through $v=0$ with $H(0)=B''(0)/2!$, and $H$ is real on the real gap.

Fix a real $v\in(-
u_0,
u_0)$, $R>
u_0+|v|$, $0<\eta<\min(1,(
u_0-|v|)/3)$, and $\delta>0$. Choose $\epsilon>0$ so the closed radius-$\epsilon$ discs about $\pm
u_0$ are disjoint, avoid the radius-$\eta$ disc about $v$, and lie strictly inside the radius-$R$ circle about $v$. Let $U_\delta=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}$, which is star-shaped by [F6]. The contour $\Gamma_{R,\eta,\epsilon}$ follows the real line left-to-right from $v-R$ to $v+R$, replacing the intervals about $v$ and $\pm
u_0$ by upper semicircles traversed left-to-right, and closes by the radius-$R$ upper semicircle traversed right-to-left. The filled function $G_\delta(z)=(H(z+i\delta)-H(v+i\delta))/(z-v)$ is continuous on $U_\delta$ and holomorphic away from $v$ by [F4].

Apply [F5] to $G_\delta$ on $\Gamma_{R,\eta,\epsilon}$. The integral of $dz/(z-v)$ over the contour without threshold detours is zero: the real-segment logarithms cancel, and the small and large semicircles contribute $-i\pi$ and $+i\pi$. Replacing a real interval about either threshold by its semicircle preserves that integral, because $1/(z-v)$ is holomorphic on a disc containing the interval and semicircle but not $v$; [F5] applied there gives equality of the two path integrals. Thus $\int_{\Gamma_{R,\eta,\epsilon}}dz/(z-v)=0$, and the definition of $G_\delta$ yields $\int_{\Gamma_{R,\eta,\epsilon}}H(z+i\delta)/(z-v)\,dz=0$.

First hold $R,\eta,\epsilon$ fixed and let $\delta\downarrow0$. The detoured contour avoids the threshold points and $v$. On each retained real cut segment $K$, the new continuous-bank hypothesis in [F1] gives uniform convergence of $H(x+i\delta)$ to $H_+(x)$. Explicitly, the integral error is at most $|K|\sup_K|H(x+i\delta)-H_+(x)|/\operatorname{dist}(K,v)$, which tends to zero. Compact gap segments and semicircles have the same uniform convergence by holomorphy, with their length and minimum distance from $v$ giving the analogous bound. Therefore the entire fixed contour integral converges to its boundary-contour value. Take imaginary parts at these fixed radii: every retained real-gap segment contributes zero because $H$ is real there. Now let $\epsilon\downarrow0$: the threshold semicircle contributions vanish by exactly the endpoint-arc hypothesis in [F1], and the retained imaginary cut integrals converge by the specified improper-bank limits. This step does not require convergence of separate real-part integrals on the gap side of a threshold. Finally let $R\to\infty$ and $\eta\downarrow0$. The outer integral has modulus at most $\pi\sup_{|z-v|=R,\,\operatorname{Im}z\ge0}|H(z)|\to0$ by the uniform high-energy bound. On the small semicircle the difference from $-i\pi H(v)$ is bounded by $\pi\sup_{|z-v|=\eta}|H(z)-H(v)|\to0$. Since $H(v)$ is real, the resulting imaginary-part identity is $H(v)=\pi^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{Im}H_+(x)/(x-v)\,dx$, with the integrand set to zero throughout the gap, including at $x=v$. Only the cut integrals remain; a full complex real-line principal value is not asserted. No dominated-convergence theorem or unasserted interchange of pointwise boundary limits is used.

On each compact interval, rho is Riemann integrable and each displayed kernel is continuous, so their products are Riemann integrable by the Darboux-oscillation estimate and uniform continuity. The kernels are bounded near threshold and by a constant times nu^-3 at infinity, so the improper integrals converge by the integral definition and comparison. Crossing and real analyticity give opposite imaginary parts on the paired cuts, yielding the twice-subtracted forward dispersion relation.

Fix arbitrary integer N>=1. The geometric-series remainder is uniformly bounded by q^(N+1)/(1-q), and after integration its contribution to B(v) is bounded by (2/pi)*v^2*q^(N+1)/(1-q)*integral rho(nu)nu^-3 dnu = O(v^(2N+4)). Thus the expansion through v^(2N+2) has remainder o(v^(2N+2)); uniqueness of the Taylor series identifies its coefficients. Since N is arbitrary, the moment formula holds for every n>=1.

For finite R, rho(nu)nu^(-2n-1) is Riemann integrable by the compact-kernel argument in step 4.1 and nonnegative, so monotonicity makes its finite integral nonnegative. Comparison with nu0^(-2n+2)rho(nu)nu^-3 gives a finite improper limit. The limit and the positive factor 2/pi prove nonnegativity; equality is allowed.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all seven steps and exact F1-F10 suppliers. Filled difference quotient is continuous on the translated upper half-plane, and Cauchy applies to the detoured contour. Real-segment logarithms and clockwise inner/counterclockwise outer arcs cancel the kernel integral. Compact-bank continuity gives uniform fixed-contour limits; endpoint caps are assumed to vanish; imaginary gap integrals vanish without asserting separate real-part convergence. Uniform o(|w|^2) kills the outer H arc. Left-bank imaginary sign is negative by evenness and reflection, yielding the plus pair of positive kernels. Product oscillation bound proves local Riemann integrability, comparison gives finite moments, and geometric remainder O(v^(2N+4)) identifies every Taylor coefficient. v=0 is filled holomorphically; rho=0 allows equality. Read source de Rham et al. equations (1)-(14), PDF pp.1-3; no physical realization inferred. Diagram orientations and revised epsilon label match the schematic with explicitly suppressed caps. Published monotonicity commentary and omitted comparison hypothesis are nonfatal to the exact F9/F10 uses, recorded separately.
